slides.title: Module 3 · Influence · Unit 6
slides.notes:
UNIT 6 · PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT SETUP
Module 3 · Influence · Unit 6

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Open the unit with its intent.
Unit 6 sets up enterprise performance management on two operating systems: people performance, what people deliver (the Human Operating System), and organisational performance, what the organisation enables through its organisational conditions (the Organisational Operating System).
Participants learn the S2R® Contribution Map™, which connects an enterprise Key Result to the contributions of business functions, people and organisational conditions, and FACES, the five functions through which those contributions are managed. In Section 5 each group builds both for its own Capstone strategy.

2. Set the tone.
Avoid: turning the Contribution Map or FACES into a compliance checklist. They are design and management tools.
Keep in view: a missed target is evidence of a performance gap; it does not establish its cause.
Probe leaders who equate "we have a scorecard" with "we have a PM system": "What happens after you look at the scorecard? What changes? Who decides what?"

slides.title: Key learning outcomes
slides.notes:
KEY LEARNING OUTCOMES (identical in the participant and facilitator files)

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Read the four outcomes.
1. Evaluate and improve performance management arrangements against strategic priorities.
2. Integrate enterprise results, leadership accountability and performance evidence into a coherent management system.
3. Apply consistent executive judgement to performance status and its strategic implications.
4. Use performance insight to improve accountability, decisions and organisational responsiveness.

Each section slide carries that section’s learning outcomes.

slides.title: The unit journey
slides.notes:
THE UNIT JOURNEY

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Walk the five sections.
Section 1 · Awareness: measurement and management, people performance and organisational performance, the S2R® Contribution Map™ and FACES.
Section 2 · Intelligence: performance management as the execution bridge, and compliance and commitment architecture.
Section 3 · Extrapolating: executive performance perspectives and the continuous performance management shift.
Section 4 · Integration: one worked example that maps the contributions to an enterprise Key Result and manages them through FACES.
Section 5 · Application: each group builds its own Contribution Map and FACES application, as Capstone work.

2. Name the questions the unit keeps asking.
"If your organisation stopped producing its performance reports tomorrow, which decisions would leaders no longer be able to make?"
"When a target is missed, how do you distinguish an individual contribution problem from an organisational delivery problem?"
"If employees are meeting their performance commitments but system outages continue to delay customer resolution, who must take responsibility for the performance gap?"

slides.title: Section 1 · Awareness — What
slides.notes:
SECTION 1 · AWARENESS — WHAT
Foundations of Enterprise Performance Management System Design
What performance management must manage: the contribution of people and the conditions the organisation provides, connected to enterprise results.

Section learning outcomes:
1. Convert performance evidence into accountable decisions and follow-through.
2. Manage human contributions and organisational conditions as interdependent drivers of results.

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Frame the section.
Say: "This section sets the foundations: what performance management is, people performance and organisational performance behind enterprise performance, the S2R® Contribution Map™ that connects them to an enterprise result, and FACES, the five functions that manage them."

slides.title: 1.1 · Measurement and management
slides.notes:
1.1 — MEASUREMENT VS MANAGEMENT (The core distinction)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Reframe performance management before you define it.
Ask leaders to clear their minds of the words "surveillance" and "pressure" and to picture the dashboard of a high-performance vehicle. A dashboard gives the driver accurate, real-time information so that they can make better decisions: whether to accelerate, adjust course, or pull over and refuel. It passes no judgement on the driver. The performance management system is the organisational equivalent: the visibility infrastructure of strategy execution.

2. Teach the distinction.
Say: "Performance management (PM) and performance measurement are distinct disciplines. Measurement answers: What happened? It provides data, results, scores and dashboards. Management answers: What do we do about it? It establishes the conversations, decisions, actions and accountability through which leaders respond to that evidence."

3. Give the example.
Say: "An organisation can measure a missed service target accurately without managing the cause. A dashboard may show that customer requests take twelve days against a standard of five. Effective management asks whether the delay reflects unclear individual expectations, insufficient capacity, a broken hand-off, slow approval rights, or a combination. Each explanation calls for a different response."

4. Ask, now that the distinction is taught.
Ask: "If your organisation stopped producing its performance reports tomorrow, which decisions would leaders no longer be able to make?"
Follow with: "When a target is missed, how do you distinguish an individual contribution problem from an organisational delivery problem?" Take two or three answers in the chat.

slides.title: 1.1 · The design sequence
slides.notes:
1.1 — THE DESIGN SEQUENCE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Teach the four steps in order.
Say: "The design sequence is deliberate: define success; design how performance will be managed; identify the evidence that management decisions require; then use that evidence to recognise contribution, correct constraints and improve delivery."
Step 1 · Define success: Agree the result the organisation must achieve.
Step 2 · Design how performance will be managed: Agree the conversations, decisions, actions and accountability that will respond to the evidence.
Step 3 · Identify the evidence that management decisions require: Collect the data the management decisions need.
Step 4 · Use the evidence: Recognise contribution, correct constraints and improve delivery.

2. Close the part.
Say: "Reports become useful because the organisation has decided who will act on them and how."

slides.title: 1.2 · Two operating systems
slides.notes:
1.2 — TWO OPERATING SYSTEMS BEHIND ENTERPRISE PERFORMANCE (Understanding what people deliver and what the organisation enables)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Open with the question.
Begin by asking participants: "When an employee or department misses a performance target, how does your organisation determine whether the problem is with individual performance or the conditions under which the work is performed?" Take two or three answers in the chat.

2. Teach why there are two systems.
Say: "Enterprise performance is the combined result of individual and collective contributions, supported by the organisational conditions required to deliver those results."
Say: "An organisation may have capable employees who consistently work towards their targets, yet still struggle to achieve its strategic outcomes. Equally, an organisation may have strong systems, sufficient resources and well-designed processes, but fail to achieve results because individuals are not delivering the contributions expected of them."
Say: "This distinction is fundamental to Enterprise Performance Management (EPM). A complete performance management system must evaluate what people contribute and whether the organisation provides the conditions necessary for those contributions to produce the intended results. We refer to these as two interconnected operating systems."

3. Teach the Human Operating System (left card).
Say: "The Human Operating System concerns the measurable performance of people within the organisation. It examines whether individuals and teams deliver the results expected of them and demonstrate the behaviours required to achieve those results. Human performance has two primary dimensions."
Performance against KPIs and objectives. Say: "These establish what an individual or team is expected to deliver. For example, a customer service employee may be expected to resolve 90% of enquiries within an agreed turnaround time, while a sales manager may be accountable for achieving a quarterly revenue target. The performance management system must establish clear targets, evidence of achievement and a consistent basis for evaluating actual performance."
They may include strategic contributions expressed through OKRs, operational outputs measured through key performance indicators (KPIs), and specific performance commitments.
Performance against behavioural expectations. Say: "These establish how individuals are expected to perform their responsibilities. For example, a manager may achieve departmental targets while consistently withholding information from other departments, undermining collaboration and delaying enterprise-wide delivery. A complete assessment must therefore consider both the results achieved and the behaviours demonstrated."
They include observable behaviours such as collaboration, accountability, adherence to organisational values, responsiveness, ethical conduct and leadership effectiveness.
The Human Operating System answers: "Are individuals and teams delivering their expected results and demonstrating the behaviours required for sustained organisational performance?"

4. Introduce the Organisational Operating System (right card).
Say: "The Organisational Operating System concerns the conditions that enable or constrain performance."
Say: "Within S2R®, these conditions are examined through ESRG: Environment, Systems, Resources and Governance. ESRG provides the structure for evaluating whether the organisation has the operating capability necessary to support its strategic ambition." The next slide takes the four elements one at a time.

slides.title: 1.2 · The Organisational Operating System · ESRG
slides.notes:
1.2 — THE ORGANISATIONAL OPERATING SYSTEM · ESRG

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Teach the four elements, one row at a time.
E · Environment. Say: "The conditions within which people and organisational processes operate. These include the working environment, organisational climate, cross-functional relationships and external operating conditions that influence delivery."
Example: a customer service team may have clear targets, but persistent conflict between departments prevents timely resolution of customer enquiries.
Performance management consideration: Are the operating conditions supporting or obstructing the achievement of expected results?

S · Systems. Say: "The processes, workflows, technologies and operating mechanisms through which work is performed. Systems determine how efficiently and reliably the organisation converts effort and resources into outputs."
Example: employees may be expected to process 100 applications daily, but an unreliable processing system limits actual throughput to 60 applications.
Performance management consideration: Are the systems and processes capable of supporting the required performance standards?

R · Resources. Say: "The people, skills, capacity, funding, equipment, information and other resources required to deliver results. Resource adequacy must be evaluated against the level of performance the organisation expects."
Example: a department may be required to double its service output while operating with the same capacity and equipment.
Performance management consideration: Does the organisation have sufficient and appropriately deployed resources to achieve its targets?

G · Governance. Say: "The decision rights, accountability arrangements, policies, controls and escalation mechanisms that guide organisational execution. Governance determines whether decisions can be made at the appropriate level and whether constraints can be resolved in time."
Example: a department may have the resources to complete a project, but repeated approval delays prevent it from meeting agreed milestones.
Performance management consideration: Do governance arrangements enable timely decisions, clear accountability and effective resolution of performance constraints?

2. Close the slide.
The Organisational Operating System answers: "Does the organisation have the environment, systems, resources and governance necessary to deliver its expected results consistently?"

slides.title: 1.2 · How the two operating systems interact
slides.notes:
1.2 — HOW THE TWO OPERATING SYSTEMS INTERACT

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Teach the interdependence.
Say: "The two systems are interdependent. Human performance measures what individuals and teams contribute. Organisational performance examines whether ESRG provides the conditions required for those contributions to produce enterprise results."

2. Use the customer service example.
Say: "Consider a customer service department with a target of resolving 90% of enquiries within 48 hours. At the end of the month, the department achieves only 65%. A conventional performance review may conclude that the employees are underperforming. An integrated EPM system examines both operating systems before determining the appropriate management response."
Read the questions on each side (Human Operating System | ESRG):
Are employees meeting their individual resolution targets? | Environment: Are cross-functional working conditions supporting timely resolution?
Are employees following the required service procedures? | Systems: Is the customer management system functioning reliably?
Are employees demonstrating accountability and responsiveness? | Resources: Is staffing capacity sufficient for the volume of enquiries?
Are team leaders meeting their supervisory commitments? | Governance: Are decisions and escalations being resolved within the required time?

3. Show the two possible findings.
Say: "The evidence may reveal that employees are performing their responsibilities correctly, but system failures and approval delays are preventing the department from achieving its targets. Alternatively, ESRG conditions may be adequate, while employees are consistently failing to meet agreed performance expectations."
Say: "Both situations produce disappointing results, but they require different management responses. This is why an enterprise performance management system must distinguish between human performance shortfalls and organisational operating constraints. It enables leaders to establish accountability fairly, direct interventions appropriately and avoid repeatedly holding individuals responsible for conditions outside their control."
Use the customer service example to demonstrate that a missed target is evidence of a performance gap, but does not automatically establish its cause.
Emphasise that leaders must examine both the contribution expected from people and the ESRG conditions required to enable delivery.

4. Teach the Enterprise Performance Principle.
Say: "Organisational performance emerges from the interaction between what individuals and teams contribute and how effectively the organisation’s Environment, Systems, Resources and Governance enable those contributions to produce results."
Say: "An integrated EPM system must therefore establish two connected lines of performance accountability. Human Performance: individual and team KPIs, OKRs and behavioural expectations. Organisational Performance: ESRG effectiveness in enabling the achievement of enterprise outcomes. Both must be visible, measured, reviewed and managed."
The central teaching point is that performance accountability must extend to those responsible for organisational operating conditions as well as those responsible for individual and team targets.

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write a personal reflection at the foot of part 1.2 (Learning Portfolio): Think of a recurring performance shortfall in your organisation. Does your current performance management system assess both dimensions, the Human Operating System and the Organisational Operating System, and assign accountability for addressing them?

slides.title: 1.3 · The S2R® Contribution Map™
slides.notes:
1.3 — THE S2R® CONTRIBUTION MAP™ (Connecting enterprise strategic outcomes to functional contributions)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Introduce the map with the customer service example.
Introduce the Contribution Map using the customer service example. Begin with the enterprise key result of improving 48-hour customer enquiry resolution from 65% to 90%.
Explain that achieving this outcome requires contributions from several functions, each with different responsibilities. Walk participants through the map, showing how Customer Service, IT, Operations and Workforce Planning contribute to the same enterprise result.

2. Teach what the map is.
Say: "The S2R® Contribution Map™ is a strategy-to-execution tool that identifies the interconnected contributions required from business functions, individuals and teams, and organisational operating conditions to achieve an enterprise strategic outcome."
Say: "It establishes a clear line of sight between the organisation’s strategic intent and the contributions required across people performance and organisational performance: people performance, the results and behaviours individuals and teams must deliver; and organisational performance, the organisational conditions (environment, systems, resources and governance) necessary to enable those contributions."
Say: "The map identifies the relationships and dependencies between functions, making visible how their combined contributions support enterprise results. Where appropriate, it also establishes measurable performance commitments or evidence that the required organisational conditions support delivery."
Say: "The central principle: enterprise results are achieved through connected human and organisational contributions, supported by clear functional accountability."

3. Teach why the map matters.
Say: "An organisation achieves its strategic results through the combined contributions of its business functions. Each function performs different activities, possesses different capabilities and carries different responsibilities. However, these contributions must ultimately support the same enterprise strategic outcomes."
Say: "A common weakness in performance management is that departments establish their own KPIs and measure their performance independently. Finance measures financial performance, HR measures people-related outcomes, IT measures technology performance, and Operations measures operational efficiency. Each department may report satisfactory performance while the organisation continues to miss its strategic targets. This happens when functional performance is managed without sufficient clarity about how the contributions connect to enterprise results."
Say: "For example, an organisation may have an enterprise objective to improve customer service. Customer Service may focus on resolving enquiries, IT on maintaining system availability, Operations on processing requests, and HR on ensuring adequate staffing. All four functions may have relevant KPIs. However, unless their contributions are connected to the enterprise objective, leaders may struggle to establish whether the combined performance of these functions is sufficient to achieve the intended result."
Say: "The S2R® Contribution Map™ provides that connection."

4. Teach the logic, one card at a time.
Step 1 · Enterprise OKR: what must the organisation achieve? Identify the agreed enterprise strategic objective and its measurable key result. This establishes the collective outcome towards which the organisation is working.
Step 2 · Required functional contributions: what must each function deliver? Identify the specific contribution each business function must make towards achieving the enterprise outcome. These contributions must reflect the interdependencies between functions.
Step 3 · Human and organisational contributions: what is required to deliver each functional contribution? For each function, identify the results and behaviours required from individuals and teams, together with measurable performance commitments wherever practical; and the specific organisational conditions necessary to enable delivery, together with appropriate performance measures or evidence that those conditions are established and functioning.
Only the organisational conditions relevant to the required contribution are included. Not every organisational condition needs a numerical metric.

5. Emphasise the three teaching points.
1. Functional KPIs must have a clear connection to enterprise outcomes. A department can perform well against its own measures without making the contribution the enterprise requires.
2. Functional contributions are interdependent. A weakness in one function can undermine the results of several others.
3. Accountability must follow the contribution. Each function must be accountable for the performance commitments it controls, while collective enterprise results remain a shared leadership responsibility.

slides.title: 1.3 · How the map connects the two systems
slides.notes:
1.3 — HOW THE CONTRIBUTION MAP CONNECTS PEOPLE PERFORMANCE AND ORGANISATIONAL PERFORMANCE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Teach the two dimensions.
Say: "The S2R® Contribution Map™ integrates people performance and organisational performance into the design of enterprise performance. For every required functional contribution, the map identifies two interconnected dimensions."
People Performance: what must people deliver? The map establishes the expected results and behaviours of individuals and teams, supported by measurable performance commitments wherever practical.
Organisational Performance: what must the organisation enable? The map identifies the specific organisational conditions necessary for people to deliver their contributions. These requirements may be expressed through numerical performance standards or other evidence of organisational readiness and effectiveness.

2. Give the IT example.
Say: "For example, maintaining reliable customer management systems requires IT employees to monitor and resolve incidents promptly. It also requires reliable infrastructure and sufficient technical support capacity. The human contribution can be assessed through incident-resolution performance. Organisational capability can be assessed through system availability and evidence of adequate technical support arrangements."
Say: "The two dimensions are connected but require distinct management attention. The Contribution Map therefore establishes what must be delivered by people, what must be enabled by the organisation, and how both contribute to the enterprise result."

3. Bridge to FACES.
Say: "The S2R® Contribution Map™ establishes what each function must contribute, what people must deliver and which organisational conditions must support their performance. It also identifies the measures and evidence required to assess these contributions."
Say: "The next challenge is to ensure that these commitments are consistently delivered and that performance gaps trigger appropriate management action. The FACES Framework establishes the five management functions required to achieve this across people performance and organisational performance."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write a personal reflection at the foot of part 1.3 (Learning Portfolio): Choose one enterprise Key Result in your own organisation. Which business functions must contribute to it? For one of those functions, what must its people deliver, and which Environment, Systems, Resources or Governance conditions must the organisation provide for that delivery? Where is the connection weakest today?

slides.title: 1.4 · The FACES framework
slides.notes:
1.4 — THE FACES FRAMEWORK (Five functions of an integrated Enterprise Performance Management system)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Teach what FACES is.
Say: "The FACES Framework defines five interconnected functions that an effective Enterprise Performance Management (EPM) system must fulfil."
Say: "Each function applies to people performance and organisational performance. People Performance: what individuals and teams deliver through their KPIs, OKRs and demonstrated behaviours. Organisational Performance: how effectively the organisational conditions enable the achievement of intended results."

2. Name the five functions on the slide.
F · Foster a Results Culture · A · Align Performance · C · Create Measurement Transparency · E · Embed Shared Accountability · S · Support Continuous Development.
The next slide sets out each function for the people and for the organisational conditions.

slides.title: 1.4 · FACES for people and organisational performance
slides.notes:
1.4 — FACES: COMPARING HUMAN AND ORGANISATIONAL PERFORMANCE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Take each function across both columns, the people first, then the organisational conditions.

F · Foster a Results Culture.
People performance. Say: "Establish a culture of individual and team performance ownership. Employees understand their targets, take responsibility for commitments and demonstrate expected behaviours. Leaders reinforce performance through regular feedback, recognition of dependable contributors and consistent responses to underperformance. Achieving results through behaviours that undermine colleagues, customers or organisational values is not acceptable performance."
Organisational performance. Say: "Establish organisational responsibility for enabling results. Leaders must demonstrate the same commitment to maintaining effective operating conditions that they expect employees to demonstrate towards their targets. Recurring system failures, inadequate resources or governance delays cannot be continually tolerated while employees are held accountable for missed results. A results culture requires leaders to address constraints in the organisational conditions that repeatedly undermine delivery."

A · Align Performance.
People performance. Say: "Connect individual and team performance to enterprise strategic outcomes. Strategic priorities must translate into meaningful KPIs, OKRs and behavioural expectations. Employees should understand how their work contributes to broader organisational results. Alignment also includes collaboration where successful delivery depends on contributions across departments."
Organisational performance. Say: "Align the organisational conditions with enterprise strategic requirements. The working environment, systems, resources and governance arrangements must be configured to support the results the organisation intends to achieve. For example, a strategic commitment to faster customer service must be supported by efficient workflows, sufficient capacity and timely decision-making. Targets become difficult to achieve when organisational capability is misaligned with strategic ambition."

C · Create Measurement Transparency.
People performance. Say: "Make performance expectations and assessment criteria clear and credible. Employees must understand their KPIs, targets, weightings, behavioural standards and rating criteria. Performance assessments should rest on observable evidence. Transparency allows employees to understand their progress and builds confidence in the fairness of performance evaluations."
Organisational performance. Say: "Make organisational performance conditions measurable and visible. Leaders need evidence of whether the organisational conditions are supporting or constraining delivery. This includes system availability, process efficiency, capacity against demand, cross-functional coordination and decision turnaround times. A missed departmental target reveals a performance gap; evidence on the organisational conditions helps establish why that gap exists and where intervention is required."

E · Embed Shared Accountability.
People performance. Say: "Clarify responsibility for individual contributions and collective results. Individuals remain accountable for their KPIs, OKRs and behaviours. Managers are accountable for setting expectations, providing feedback and addressing performance concerns. Where results require teamwork, each person’s contribution and responsibilities must be clear. Shared accountability should strengthen ownership without making responsibility ambiguous."
Organisational performance. Say: "Assign accountability for organisational enablement and constraint resolution. Responsibility for each organisational condition must sit with the appropriate leader. Operations may own process efficiency, IT may own system reliability, resource owners may own capacity, and executives may own governance decisions. Where one function’s performance depends on another, the dependency, accountable owner and escalation arrangements must be explicit. This forms part of the foundation for the S2R® Contribution Map™."

S · Support Continuous Development.
People performance. Say: "Use performance evidence to strengthen individual and team capability. Reviews should identify development needs linked to actual performance requirements. These may include technical skills, planning, decision-making, leadership, collaboration or behavioural improvement. Development actions should have clear objectives and follow-up reviews to determine whether performance has improved."
Organisational performance. Say: "Use performance evidence to strengthen organisational operating capability. Recurring constraints in the organisational conditions should trigger improvements to workflows, technologies, resource allocation, operating conditions or governance arrangements. For example, repeated approval delays may require redesigned decision rights, while persistent capacity shortages may require resource reallocation. Organisational improvement must be monitored to establish whether the intervention strengthens delivery."

slides.title: 1.4 · When the enterprise result falls short
slides.notes:
1.4 — HOW FACES WORKS WHEN THE ENTERPRISE RESULT FALLS SHORT

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Set the scene.
Say: "Assume the organisation reviews its performance and finds that only 65% of customer enquiries are being resolved within 48 hours, against the year-end target of 90%. The review reveals different performance conditions across the four functions."

2. Walk through the four functions.
Walk participants through the four functions, showing how the same FACES principles are applied differently according to the contributions required.
Customer Service. Evidence: Follow-through on outstanding enquiries is below the agreed standard. How FACES is applied: Outstanding cases are reviewed against assigned responsibilities. Employees receive feedback on missed commitments, recurring obstacles are escalated, and subsequent follow-through results establish whether performance is improving.
IT. Evidence: Incident-response commitments are being achieved, but system availability remains below the required standard. How FACES is applied: Incident-response performance and system availability are examined separately. IT leadership investigates recurring outages, assigns responsibility for correcting the underlying infrastructure problems and reviews subsequent availability results.
Operations. Evidence: Processing performance is affected by approval delays and some employee processing gaps. How FACES is applied: Processing records distinguish employee-related delays from approval bottlenecks. Employees receive support where performance gaps are identified, while the appropriate decision owners review approval arrangements that are slowing delivery.
HR / Workforce Planning. Evidence: Staffing schedules are completed as required, but actual staffing coverage remains insufficient. How FACES is applied: Completed schedules are compared with actual staffing requirements. Workforce Planning coordinates available staffing adjustments, while unresolved capacity requirements are submitted to the appropriate resource decision-makers.

3. Draw the distinction.
Draw attention to the distinction between people performance accountability and organisational enablement accountability.

4. Conclude by reinforcing the connection.
Say: "The S2R® Contribution Map™ establishes the contributions, performance measures and enabling conditions required for enterprise results. FACES establishes the management disciplines through which those contributions are aligned, evaluated, acted upon and continuously strengthened."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write a personal reflection at the foot of part 1.4 (Learning Portfolio): For the Key Result you chose in part 1.3: which FACES function is weakest in the way your organisation manages these contributions today, for the people and for the organisational conditions? Which one management arrangement would strengthen it?

slides.notes:
SECTION 1 REFLECTIONS

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Show the slide and read the three prompts aloud.
