1.3 Reflection — Contributions in Your Organisation: "Choose one enterprise Key Result in your own organisation. Which business functions must contribute to it? For one of those functions, what must its people deliver, and which Environment, Systems, Resources or Governance conditions must the organisation provide for that delivery? Where is the connection weakest today?"
1.4 Reflection — FACES in Your Organisation: "For the Key Result you chose in part 1.3: which FACES function is weakest in the way your organisation manages these contributions today, for the people and for the organisational conditions? Which one management arrangement would strengthen it?"

2. Say what the reflections are for.
Say: "These reflections are personal. Name one real, recurring shortfall and look at whether your system covers the people and the organisational conditions. Then map one of your own organisation’s Key Results the way the Contribution Map does, and look at how your organisation manages those contributions through FACES."

3. Bridge to Section 2.
Say: "You now know what must be managed. Section 2 shows how performance management keeps strategy connected to performance throughout delivery."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write these personal reflections at the foot of parts 1.2, 1.3 and 1.4 of the participant file. They go into their Learning Portfolio when they submit the unit.

slides.title: Section 2 · Intelligence — Why
slides.notes:
SECTION 2 · INTELLIGENCE — WHY
Performance Management as the Execution Bridge
Understanding why enterprise performance depends on connecting strategic outcomes, human contributions and organisational operating capability through an integrated management system.

Section learning outcomes:
1. Establish management disciplines that sustain the connection between strategy and performance.
2. Evaluate whether performance practices build genuine commitment or merely compliance.

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Frame the section.
Say: "Section 1 set out what must be managed. Section 2 explains why performance management is the bridge that keeps strategy connected to performance throughout delivery, and how the architecture you choose shapes accountability."

slides.title: 2.1 · Performance management as the execution bridge
slides.notes:
2.1 — PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT AS THE EXECUTION BRIDGE (Four execution bridges)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Name the challenge.
Say: "The S2R® Contribution Map™ establishes the contributions required to achieve enterprise results. FACES defines the five functions through which human and organisational performance are managed. The next challenge is sustaining the connection between these contributions and the intended results throughout execution."
Say: "Strategy is delivered over time. Performance expectations must remain clear, progress must be visible, and emerging gaps must lead to timely management responses. Without these disciplines, the connection between strategic intent and actual delivery gradually weakens."
Without this bridge, organisations generate what might be called random acts of excellence: genuine effort, real capability, strong intentions, none of which reliably move the needle.

2. Teach the bridge.
Say: "This is why performance management serves as an execution bridge: it provides the disciplines that keep strategy connected to performance throughout delivery."

3. Teach the four bridges, one row at a time.
Bridge 1 · Decomposing the Big Picture: Connecting strategic outcomes to actionable performance expectations.
Bridge 2 · Defining the Logic of Success: Establishing how successful performance is understood and evaluated.
Bridge 3 · Calibrating the Rhythm: Maintaining visibility of progress throughout the execution period.
Bridge 4 · Structuring the Dialogue: Converting performance evidence into decisions and action.
Say: "Together, these bridges explain why performance management is essential to sustaining the connection between strategy, human contribution, organisational capability and enterprise results."

slides.title: 2.1 · How the four bridges work together
slides.notes:
2.1.1 — HOW THE FOUR EXECUTION BRIDGES WORK TOGETHER

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Frame the slide.
Say: "The four bridges work together to sustain the connection between strategy and results. Each addresses a particular risk that can weaken execution across people performance and organisational performance."
Take the bridges one at a time through the table: why each matters, what it sustains for the people, what it sustains for the organisational conditions, and what happens when it weakens.

2. Teach each bridge.

Bridge 1. Decomposing the Big Picture.
Why it matters. Say: "Enterprise strategy must remain connected to the contributions through which it is delivered. As priorities and operating demands change, the relationship between functional performance and enterprise outcomes must remain clear."
People performance: Maintains the line of sight between enterprise objectives and individual or team expectations. Employees understand how their contributions support the intended result, including where delivery depends on other functions.
Organisational performance: Maintains alignment between strategic requirements and the organisational conditions needed to support them. Systems, resources, workflows and decision arrangements must remain appropriate to the demands of execution.
What happens when the bridge weakens: Functions become increasingly focused on their own activities and targets. Individual performance may appear satisfactory while the collective contribution to enterprise results weakens.

Bridge 2. Defining the Logic of Success.
Why it matters. Say: "Performance must be evaluated against a shared understanding of successful delivery. Completing an activity or achieving an isolated target does not necessarily establish that the intended contribution has been achieved."
People performance: Establishes clear expectations for results, performance standards, behaviours and evidence of achievement. Employees and managers have a credible basis for evaluating contribution.
Organisational performance: Establishes how effective organisational enablement will be recognised. Relevant organisational conditions are assessed through appropriate measures or qualitative evidence of their effectiveness.
What happens when the bridge weakens: Different functions interpret success differently. People performance may be rated positively while organisational constraints remain unresolved, creating a misleading picture of execution readiness and achievement.

Bridge 3. Calibrating the Rhythm.
Why it matters. Say: "Execution unfolds over time. Changes in performance, demand and operating conditions must become visible early enough for leaders to influence the outcome."
People performance: Provides regular visibility of individual and team progress, emerging performance gaps and development needs. Review frequency reflects the nature of the contribution and its effect on results.
Organisational performance: Provides visibility of changing organisational conditions, such as system reliability, staffing capacity, process efficiency and decision delays. Monitoring frequency reflects the nature and significance of each condition.
What happens when the bridge weakens: Performance deterioration is recognised too late. Employees continue working against targets while emerging organisational constraints accumulate, leaving limited opportunity for recovery.

Bridge 4. Structuring the Dialogue.
Why it matters. Say: "Performance evidence creates value when it informs decisions and action. Reviews must establish what is influencing results, who is responsible and what response is required."
People performance: Enables evidence-based conversations about contribution, achievement, behaviour, performance gaps and improvement. Employees and managers establish appropriate responses and follow-through.
Organisational performance: Enables leaders to examine constraints in the organisational conditions, determine their effect on delivery and assign decisions or interventions to the appropriate leaders. Cross-functional dependencies are addressed collectively.
What happens when the bridge weakens: Performance meetings become reporting exercises. The same gaps recur because evidence does not consistently lead to decisions, coordinated interventions and accountable follow-through.

3. Ask, now that the bridges are taught.
Ask: "Which of the four bridges is weakest in your organisation, and what do you see happening as a result?" Take two or three answers in the chat.

slides.title: 2.2 · Compliance and commitment architecture
slides.notes:
2.2 — COMPLIANCE VS COMMITMENT ARCHITECTURE (The design choice that shapes performance behaviour)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Name the design choice.
Teach the two architectures first, then the four dimensions, then how each applies to the people and to the organisational conditions.
Say: "The four execution bridges establish the disciplines required to sustain the connection between strategy and results. However, their effectiveness is influenced by the way an organisation approaches performance expectations, accountability and performance conversations. This introduces an important distinction between compliance-driven and commitment-driven performance management architectures."

2. Teach the two architectures.
A compliance-driven architecture emphasises adherence to prescribed expectations, monitoring performance and correcting deviations.
A commitment-driven architecture emphasises shared understanding of expected results, ownership of contributions, constructive performance dialogue and collective responsibility for improvement.
Say: "Both approaches recognise the importance of standards and accountability. Their differences become visible in how performance is experienced and how the organisation responds when results fall short."

3. Teach the four dimensions, one row at a time.
Purpose. Compliance-driven: Ensure minimum standards are met and deviations corrected. Commitment-driven: Generate shared ownership of results and continuous improvement.
Ownership. Compliance-driven: Leader holds accountability; team is subject to it. Commitment-driven: Team co-owns accountability; leader facilitates.
Tone. Compliance-driven: Assessment and judgement; hierarchical. Commitment-driven: Inquiry and problem-solving; collaborative.
PM Experience. Compliance-driven: Anxiety-producing; done to the individual. Commitment-driven: Energy-generating; done with the individual.

slides.title: 2.2 · Accountability for people and organisational performance
slides.notes:
2.2.2 — ACCOUNTABILITY FOR PEOPLE PERFORMANCE AND ORGANISATIONAL PERFORMANCE

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Apply the distinction to both systems.
Say: "The distinction between compliance and commitment applies to both human and organisational performance."
People performance. Say: "A compliance-driven approach tends to emphasise whether employees have met prescribed KPIs, OKRs and behavioural standards. A commitment-driven approach maintains these expectations while strengthening employees’ understanding of their contribution, ownership of results and participation in performance improvement."
Organisational performance. Say: "A compliance-driven approach may establish requirements for systems, resources, processes and governance, but concentrate primarily on whether prescribed arrangements have been followed. A commitment-driven approach also examines whether those arrangements are effective in supporting the intended results and whether emerging constraints are being addressed."

2. Show why it matters when performance falls short.
Say: "This distinction becomes particularly important when performance falls short. An employee may miss a target because of inadequate follow-through, an organisational constraint or a combination of both. A credible performance management system distinguishes between these causes before determining the appropriate response."
Say: "Commitment strengthens accountability when employees remain responsible for their contributions and organisational leaders remain equally responsible for the enabling conditions within their authority."

3. Ask, now that the architectures are taught.
Ask: "When a target is missed in your organisation, which of the two architectures does the review conversation sound like?" Take two or three answers in the chat.

slides.title: Section 3 · Extrapolating — Where
slides.notes:
SECTION 3 · EXTRAPOLATING — WHERE
Executive Performance Integration and the Evolution of Performance Management
Where does enterprise performance management become vulnerable? How executive performance perspectives and the evolution of performance management practice shape what leaders see and how they respond.

Section learning outcomes:
1. Diagnose executive performance blind spots and determine corrective responses.
2. Redesign performance practices towards continuous, developmental and team-based management.

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Frame the section.
Say: "Section 2 established the four execution bridges that sustain the connection between strategy and results. It also examined how compliance-driven and commitment-driven approaches influence accountability, performance behaviour and management responses."
Say: "Section 3 examines where enterprise performance management becomes vulnerable, through two areas: Unity in Diversity, how executive performance perspectives influence what leaders notice, prioritise and interpret; and the Continuous Performance Management Shift, how performance management practices are evolving to strengthen timely feedback, development and collective performance."

slides.title: 3.1 · Unity in Diversity: executive performance perspectives
slides.notes:
3.1 — UNITY IN DIVERSITY: EXECUTIVE PERFORMANCE PERSPECTIVES (Different executive perspectives, one enterprise result)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Teach functional bias first.
Teach functional bias first: what executives notice, prioritise and interpret.
Say: "Enterprise performance management depends on the collective contribution of executive leaders who hold different responsibilities. Each executive function develops a particular understanding of performance based on its mandate, expertise, operating priorities and the evidence it routinely examines. These perspectives are necessary because enterprise performance is multidimensional."
Say: "This reflects the principle of functional bias, introduced earlier in CESI: leaders may interpret organisational situations primarily through the priorities and assumptions associated with their professional responsibilities."
Within enterprise performance management, functional bias can influence what executives notice (the performance indicators and developments that attract their attention), what executives prioritise (the results, risks and improvements they consider most important) and how executives interpret evidence (the conclusions they draw about organisational performance and its underlying causes).

2. Name Unity in Diversity.
Say: "The challenge for executive teams is to bring these perspectives together so that functional performance information supports a coherent understanding of enterprise results."
Say: "Unity in Diversity means integrating different executive performance perspectives into one collective understanding of enterprise progress."

3. Teach what the executive team must establish.
Say: "The executive team must establish whether the performance reported by individual functions is sufficient to produce the intended collective outcome. This requires attention to people performance and organisational performance."
People performance. Say: "Executives examine whether individuals and teams are delivering their agreed KPIs, OKRs and behavioural expectations. They also consider whether the required contributions are being coordinated effectively across functions."
Organisational performance. Say: "Executives examine whether the relevant organisational conditions are enabling those contributions. Where organisational constraints affect delivery, the appropriate executive owners must take responsibility for resolving them."
Enterprise Integration. The executive team brings the evidence together to determine whether functional performance is supporting the intended enterprise result; where human contribution or organisational capability is weakening delivery; and which executive decisions or coordinated interventions are required.
Say: "The S2R® Contribution Map™ provides the established relationships between contributions. The four execution bridges provide the disciplines for sustaining those relationships. Executive integration ensures that the resulting performance evidence is interpreted and acted upon collectively."
Key insight. Say: "Executive performance integration requires leaders to recognise the limits of their functional perspectives and use collective performance evidence to make decisions in the interests of enterprise results."

slides.title: 3.1 · The ten executive performance hot zones
slides.notes:
3.1.1 — THE TEN EXECUTIVE PERFORMANCE HOT ZONES

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Frame the slide.
Say: "The ten executive performance perspectives show the blind spots each may create and the integration required to support enterprise results."
Then open the role cards, starting with the CEO, and read the natural focus, the blind spot and the integration requirement of each.

2. Teach each role, one row at a time.

CEO — Chief Executive Officer.
Natural performance focus: Enterprise results, strategic priorities, organisational performance and long-term sustainability.
Potential performance blind spot: Accepting positive functional performance reports without establishing whether their combined contributions are producing the intended enterprise outcomes.
Enterprise integration requirement: Integrate functional performance evidence into a coherent view of strategic progress. Identify where collective performance is weakening and coordinate executive responses.

CFO — Chief Financial Officer.
Natural performance focus: Financial performance, profitability, cost efficiency, cash flow and returns on investment.
Potential performance blind spot: Interpreting cost containment or favourable financial variances as success when resource constraints are weakening delivery capability.
Enterprise integration requirement: Establish whether financial decisions and resource allocations sustain the organisational capability required to achieve strategic results.

COO — Chief Operating Officer.
Natural performance focus: Operational efficiency, productivity, throughput, quality and delivery reliability.
Potential performance blind spot: Concentrating on operational efficiency and output targets without establishing whether these outputs are producing the intended customer or enterprise outcomes.
Enterprise integration requirement: Connect operational performance to strategic outcomes and examine dependencies affecting delivery across functions.

CHRO — Chief Human Resources Officer.
Natural performance focus: Employee performance, workforce capability, leadership effectiveness, engagement and organisational culture.
Potential performance blind spot: Concentrating on individual performance achievement, employee development or HR process completion while organisational conditions continue to constrain delivery.
Enterprise integration requirement: Interpret people performance evidence alongside relevant organisational conditions. Establish whether workforce capability and organisational arrangements support the results expected from people.

CIO/CTO — Chief Information/Technology Officer.
Natural performance focus: System reliability, technology performance, digital capability, cybersecurity and information infrastructure.
Potential performance blind spot: Reporting satisfactory technical performance without establishing whether technology is effectively enabling business processes and strategic delivery requirements.
Enterprise integration requirement: Connect technology measures to the operating requirements of dependent functions and the enterprise outcomes those functions support.

CMO — Chief Marketing Officer.
Natural performance focus: Market positioning, brand performance, customer engagement, acquisition and market response.
Potential performance blind spot: Interpreting strong campaign results, engagement or customer acquisition as success without establishing whether the organisation can deliver and sustain the value promised.
Enterprise integration requirement: Connect market performance to customer experience, operational delivery capability and the organisation’s strategic value proposition.

CCO — Chief Commercial Officer.
Natural performance focus: Revenue growth, sales conversion, commercial pipeline, customer retention and commercial relationships.
Potential performance blind spot: Prioritising sales volumes or revenue targets without adequately considering delivery capacity, profitability or the organisation’s ability to fulfil commitments.
Enterprise integration requirement: Connect commercial performance to financial sustainability, operational capability and customer value delivery.

CPO — Chief Procurement Officer.
Natural performance focus: Procurement efficiency, supplier performance, purchasing costs, supply reliability and contract management.
Potential performance blind spot: Prioritising purchasing savings or procurement compliance while overlooking the effects of supplier quality, availability or lead times on operational delivery.
Enterprise integration requirement: Establish whether procurement decisions and supplier arrangements support the quality, reliability and timing required for enterprise performance.

CRO — Chief Risk Officer.
Natural performance focus: Risk exposure, regulatory compliance, internal controls and governance effectiveness.
Potential performance blind spot: Concentrating on control compliance or risk avoidance without adequately examining whether governance arrangements are enabling timely and effective execution.
Enterprise integration requirement: Balance risk management requirements with the decision rights, controls and escalation arrangements necessary for reliable delivery.

CSO — Chief Strategy Officer.
Natural performance focus: Strategic alignment, strategic initiatives, portfolio priorities and long-term organisational direction.
Potential performance blind spot: Concentrating on strategic milestones, initiative completion or reported alignment without establishing whether execution is producing the intended strategic outcomes.
Enterprise integration requirement: Connect strategic progress reporting to actual enterprise results, functional contributions and the organisational conditions influencing delivery.

Executive titles and responsibilities vary between organisations. The table illustrates functional perspectives. Each organisation reads it against its own executive structure.

3. Ask, now that the hot zones are taught.
Ask: "Which blind spot do you recognise in your own executive team, and what does it cost the enterprise result?" Take two or three answers in the chat.

slides.title: 3.2 · The continuous PM shift
slides.notes:
3.2 — THE CONTINUOUS PERFORMANCE MANAGEMENT SHIFT (How performance management practices are evolving)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Name the shift.
Say: "Organisations are increasingly recognising the limitations of performance management systems built primarily around periodic assessments and individual ratings. Three important shifts are influencing how performance management is approached."

2. Walk through the three shifts, then the implication of each for people performance and organisational performance.
Shift 1 · From Annual to Continuous. Traditional orientation: Performance is formally evaluated at annual or biannual intervals. Evolving orientation: Regular check-ins, periodic reviews and timely feedback support performance throughout execution. Implication for people performance and organisational performance: Human contributions and relevant organisational conditions are reviewed frequently enough to identify emerging gaps and influence results.
Shift 2 · From Rating-Centric to Development-Centric. Traditional orientation: Performance conversations concentrate heavily on ratings and historical achievement. Evolving orientation: Performance evidence informs development, capability strengthening and future improvement. Implication for people performance and organisational performance: Individual development is considered alongside improvements to organisational processes, systems, resources and governance arrangements.
Shift 3 · From Individual to Team Performance. Traditional orientation: Performance assessment concentrates primarily on individual achievement. Evolving orientation: Individual accountability is complemented by attention to team and cross-functional contributions. Implication for people performance and organisational performance: Human collaboration and organisational dependencies become more visible within the performance management system.

3. Broaden the conversation.
Say: "These developments reinforce the importance of managing performance while execution is unfolding. They also broaden the performance management conversation."
Employee development remains important, but organisations must also improve the operating conditions that influence performance.
Individual accountability remains necessary, but enterprise results often require coordinated contributions across teams and functions.
Periodic assessments remain relevant, but they must be supported by timely performance conversations that allow leaders to respond to emerging challenges.
Key insight. Say: "Continuous performance management strengthens the organisation’s ability to recognise, interpret and respond to performance conditions while there is still an opportunity to influence results."

4. Ask, now that the shifts are taught.
Ask: "Where does your organisation sit on each of the three shifts today?" Take two or three answers in the chat.

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write a personal reflection at the foot of part 3.2 (Learning Portfolio): What is the current PM architecture of your organisation? Which PM system is currently being used?

slides.title: Section 3 Reflections
slides.notes:
SECTION 3 REFLECTIONS

HOW TO USE THIS SLIDE:

1. Show the slide and read the prompt aloud.
3.2 Reflection — Your Current PM System: "What is the current PM architecture of your organisation? Which PM system is currently being used?"

2. Say what the reflection is for.
Say: "Describe the architecture you actually have today, against the three shifts, and name the system your organisation uses."

3. Bridge to Section 4.
Say: "Section 4 brings the unit together in one worked example: the contributions an enterprise Key Result requires, and how FACES manages them."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants write this personal reflection at the foot of part 3.2 of the participant file. It goes into their Learning Portfolio when they submit the unit.

slides.title: Section 4 · Integration — Collective
slides.notes:
SECTION 4 · INTEGRATION — COLLECTIVE
Integration of Human and Organisational Performance
One worked example brings the unit together: the contributions an enterprise Key Result requires, mapped across four functions, and how FACES manages them.

Section learning outcomes:
1. Map the functional, human and organisational contributions required for enterprise results.
2. Coordinate cross-functional contributions and enabling conditions towards shared results.

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Frame the section.
Say: "The previous sections established the foundations of enterprise performance management, the disciplines that sustain execution and the importance of integrating executive performance perspectives. We now bring these concepts together through a worked example."

slides.title: 4.1 · Mapping the contributions: customer service
slides.notes:
4.1 — MAPPING THE CONTRIBUTIONS REQUIRED FOR ENTERPRISE RESULTS (Worked example: improving customer service)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Frame the worked example.
Say: "The S2R® Contribution Map™ establishes the interconnected contributions required to achieve an enterprise result. It identifies what each function must deliver, the performance expected from individuals and teams, and the organisational conditions necessary to enable those contributions. The following example demonstrates how these requirements are connected across four business functions."

2. Establish the enterprise result.
Enterprise Objective: Deliver a reliable and responsive customer service experience.
Begin with the enterprise key result: "Increase customer enquiries resolved within 48 hours from 65% to 90% by year-end."
Ask: "Which functions must contribute to achieving this result?" Draw attention to Customer Service, IT, Operations and Workforce Planning.

3. Walk through the Contribution Map.
Use Customer Service to demonstrate the distinction between the functional contribution, people performance and organisational enablement. Emphasise that the enterprise target covers all customer enquiries, while the employee resolution measure covers enquiries within employees’ control. Then examine the remaining functions, highlighting how their contributions support the same enterprise result.

Customer Service.
Required functional contribution: Resolve customer enquiries accurately and within 48 hours.
People performance, required contribution: Employees resolve assigned enquiries, follow up on outstanding cases and escalate delays requiring support from other functions.
People performance metric: Resolution: ≥90% of enquiries within employees’ control resolved within 48 hours. Follow-through: ≥95% of outstanding enquiries followed up within the agreed period.
Required organisational condition: Systems: An enquiry management system that records ownership, progress and resolution times. Governance: Clear escalation authority for enquiries requiring decisions outside Customer Service.
Organisational conditions, measure or evidence of readiness: Systems: Enquiry records provide complete timestamps and assigned ownership. Governance: Documented escalation routes and named decision owners.

IT.
Required functional contribution: Maintain reliable customer management systems to support uninterrupted enquiry processing.
People performance, required contribution: IT employees monitor system performance, respond to incidents and restore disrupted services.
People performance metric: Incident resolution: ≥95% of critical incidents resolved within two hours. Communication: ≥95% of confirmed critical incidents communicated to affected departments within 15 minutes.
Required organisational condition: Systems: Reliable infrastructure and monitoring capability to maintain system availability. Resources: Sufficient technical support coverage during service hours.
Organisational conditions, measure or evidence of readiness: Systems: ≥99% customer management system availability during service hours. Resources: Approved technical support roster covering required service hours.

Operations.
Required functional contribution: Complete internal processing and approvals within the turnaround required for customer resolution.
People performance, required contribution: Employees process assigned requests accurately and escalate exceptions that could delay customer resolution.
People performance metric: Turnaround: ≥95% of assigned requests completed within eight working hours. Accuracy: ≥98% processing accuracy.
Required organisational condition: Governance: Approval authority must be assigned at the appropriate level to prevent avoidable delays. Systems: Processing workflows must support timely handovers between Operations and Customer Service.
Organisational conditions, measure or evidence of readiness: Governance: Documented approval limits and designated decision owners. Systems: ≥95% of internal processing requests completed within the agreed turnaround time.

HR / Workforce Planning.
Required functional contribution: Ensure customer-facing operations have sufficient staffing capacity and capabilities to meet enquiry demand.
People performance, required contribution: Workforce Planning employees forecast staffing requirements, prepare schedules and coordinate responses to identified capacity gaps.
People performance metric: Planning: 100% of staffing schedules completed before the agreed deadline. Responsiveness: ≥95% of identified staffing gaps addressed within the agreed response period.
Required organisational condition: Resources: Sufficient qualified staff available to meet forecast customer enquiry volumes. Governance: Authority to approve staffing adjustments when demand exceeds available capacity.
Organisational conditions, measure or evidence of readiness: Resources: ≥95% staffing coverage against demand-based requirements. Governance: Agreed staffing adjustment authority and escalation arrangements.

Performance targets are illustrative. The purpose is to establish sufficient evidence to determine whether the required contribution is being delivered and whether the organisation is enabling it.

4. Examine the measures.
Ask: "Why do we measure both employee incident-response performance and system availability in IT?" Guide participants to recognise that employees may fulfil their responsibilities while the underlying organisational capability remains inadequate.

5. Consolidate the learning.
Say: "The Contribution Map gives us an integrated view of what must be delivered and enabled across the organisation. It establishes the performance requirements against which contributions can be assessed."

slides.title: 4.1 · Interpreting the Contribution Map
slides.notes:
4.1.2 — INTERPRETING THE CONTRIBUTION MAP

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Teach the three elements, one card at a time.
Say: "The Contribution Map establishes the relationship between three elements."
1 · Functional contribution: what must the function deliver? Each function has a defined contribution to the enterprise key result.
2 · People performance: what must individuals and teams deliver? The map identifies the results and behaviours required from people, supported by measurable performance expectations wherever practical.
3 · Organisational performance: what conditions must the organisation provide? The map identifies the relevant organisational conditions necessary to enable the human contribution.

2. Close on the measures for the organisational conditions.
Say: "Only the organisational conditions that materially affect delivery are included. Some require numerical performance measures, such as system availability or staffing coverage. Others require evidence that an arrangement or capability exists and is functioning, such as documented approval authority or established escalation procedures."

slides.title: 4.2 · Managing the contributions through FACES
slides.notes:
4.2 — MANAGING THE CONTRIBUTIONS THROUGH FACES (Applying FACES across the four functions)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Connect FACES to the Contribution Map.
Say: "The Contribution Map™ has established the contributions required from Customer Service, IT, Operations and Workforce Planning, including the expected people performance and the organisational conditions necessary to enable delivery. The following example demonstrates how each FACES function is achieved in practice across the four business functions."
Say: "In the first part of this example, we established what each function must contribute and what the organisation must enable. We now examine how these contributions are managed. FACES provides the five management functions required to sustain delivery."
Say: "The next requirement is to manage these contributions consistently throughout execution. FACES provides the five management functions through which performance expectations are aligned, evidence is examined, accountability is maintained and improvement is supported."

2. Demonstrate how FACES operates across functions.
Begin with Customer Service and work through the five FACES functions. Then select IT to demonstrate how the same management functions apply to different performance responsibilities. Emphasise that FACES applies to both employee contributions and organisational enabling conditions.

F · Foster a Results Culture.
Customer Service: Customer enquiries have clear ownership through to resolution. Employees discuss outstanding commitments, explain delays and recognise colleagues who consistently deliver reliable service. Managers demonstrate the same ownership by addressing obstacles raised by their teams.
IT: System incidents are openly reviewed to understand what happened, how the team responded and what must improve. Employees raise emerging reliability risks early, while IT leadership follows through on recurring infrastructure problems.
Operations: Processing delays and errors are discussed openly, with attention to their consequences for customer resolution. Employees raise potential bottlenecks early, and managers respond to reported constraints so that they do not recur.
HR / Workforce Planning: Staffing gaps are discussed as performance risks requiring action. Workforce Planning and operational managers jointly examine whether available capacity can meet expected demand and raise emerging shortages before service delivery is affected.

A · Align Performance.
Customer Service: Individual resolution and follow-through commitments are linked to the enterprise 48-hour target. The enquiry management system and escalation arrangements are checked against the requirements for timely resolution.
IT: Incident-resolution and communication commitments are linked to the required system availability. Technical support arrangements are matched to the service hours and reliability requirements established in the Contribution Map.
Operations: Processing turnaround and accuracy expectations are agreed in relation to the time available for customer enquiry resolution. Workflows and approval authority are checked to ensure they support the required turnaround.
HR / Workforce Planning: Staffing forecasts and schedules are based on expected enquiry volumes and the service capacity required. Staffing coverage requirements are agreed with the operational functions that depend on them.

C · Create Measurement Transparency.
Customer Service: Resolution and follow-through results are visible against agreed standards. Outstanding enquiries show their assigned owners, elapsed time and any unresolved dependencies on other functions.
IT: Incident-response results and system availability are reported together. The evidence distinguishes how effectively employees respond to incidents from whether the infrastructure is delivering the required reliability.
Operations: Processing reports show turnaround, accuracy and the causes of delays. Approval waiting times are visible alongside employee processing performance.
HR / Workforce Planning: Staffing schedules, forecast demand and actual staffing coverage are reviewed together. The evidence shows whether scheduling commitments have been fulfilled and whether sufficient qualified employees are available.

E · Embed Shared Accountability.
Customer Service: Each enquiry has an assigned owner responsible for follow-through. Delays requiring IT, Operations or staffing support are recorded against the responsible function, with agreed escalation and resolution arrangements.
IT: Incident owners are responsible for response and communication commitments. IT leadership is responsible for system reliability and for securing decisions or resources needed to correct infrastructure constraints.
Operations: Processing responsibilities are assigned to employees and supervisors. Approval delays are referred to the managers who control the relevant decision rights, with unresolved constraints escalated to the Operations Executive.
HR / Workforce Planning: Workforce Planning is responsible for forecasts, schedules and coordinating staffing adjustments. Operational managers confirm their staffing requirements, while decisions on additional capacity are referred to the appropriate resource authority.

S · Support Continuous Development.
Customer Service: Repeated follow-through gaps are examined using actual enquiry records. Coaching addresses employee capability gaps, while recurring problems with case tracking or escalation lead to improvements in the supporting arrangements. Subsequent results establish whether performance has improved.
IT: Incident trends identify technical skills requiring development and recurring infrastructure weaknesses requiring correction. Subsequent incident-response and availability results show whether the improvements have strengthened service reliability.
Operations: Processing errors inform targeted employee development. Recurring workflow and approval delays inform process or governance improvements. Changes are evaluated against turnaround and accuracy performance.
HR / Workforce Planning: Differences between forecast and actual demand inform improvements to workforce planning. Recurring staffing shortages lead to adjustments in scheduling, deployment or capacity arrangements, with staffing coverage used to evaluate their effectiveness.

3. Examine shared accountability.
Ask: "If Customer Service employees are meeting their performance commitments but system outages continue to delay customer resolution, who must take responsibility for the performance gap?" Guide participants to distinguish employee accountability from the organisational responsibility for system reliability.

4. Connect management action to improvement.
Ask: "What should happen when performance reviews repeatedly identify the same approval delays or staffing shortages?" Emphasise that performance management must lead to appropriate decisions, assigned responsibilities and follow-through.

5. Interpret the worked example (the five rows on the slide).
Say: "FACES operates through five connected disciplines."
Foster: Performance commitments and delivery obstacles are discussed openly, with consistent follow-through from employees and leaders.
Align: Human contributions and organisational conditions are connected to the requirements of the enterprise key result.
Create Measurement Transparency: Performance evidence makes both employee contributions and organisational constraints visible.
Embed Shared Accountability: Responsibilities for delivering contributions and resolving constraints are assigned to the people and functions with the relevant authority.
Support Continuous Development: Performance findings lead to improvements in employee capability and organisational operating conditions, with subsequent results used to evaluate progress.
Say: "Together, these disciplines ensure that the contributions established in the S2R® Contribution Map™ are actively managed towards the enterprise result."

6. Consolidate the learning.
Say: "The Contribution Map establishes the contributions, performance measures and enabling conditions required for enterprise results. FACES establishes the management disciplines through which those contributions are aligned, evaluated, acted upon and continuously strengthened."

slides.title: Section 5 · Application — In Practice
slides.notes:
SECTION 5 · APPLICATION — IN PRACTICE
Building Your Enterprise Performance Management System
Application · Each group builds three connected components of the Enterprise Performance Management System for the strategy in its Capstone Blueprint: the S2R® Contribution Map™, the FACES application and the WARD check-up for its enterprise Key Result.

Section learning outcomes:
1. Design the contribution arrangements required to deliver a chosen enterprise Key Result.
2. Establish shared management accountability for contributions across functions.

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Frame the application.
Say: "You have already established your capstone organisation’s strategic direction, strategic objectives and Key Results. In this application, your group uses that work to develop three connected components of your Enterprise Performance Management System: Activity 1, the S2R® Contribution Map™, Activity 2, the FACES application, and Activity 3, the WARD check-up for your enterprise Key Result."
Order: all three activities are group work and Capstone work. Activity 1 needs the group’s confirmed Enterprise OKRs from Unit 3, part 5.2. Activity 2 uses the business functions the group names in Activity 1. Activity 3 sets the WARD check-up for the Key Result chosen in Activity 1, using the conditions named in the Contribution Map.
How to guide the work: brief each activity from the worked example in Section 4, then let the groups work through the steps on their own pages. The group chooses its scribe; the entries appear on every member’s page.

slides.title: 5.1 · Activity 1: Build your S2R® Contribution Map™
slides.notes:
5.1 — ACTIVITY 1: BUILD YOUR S2R® CONTRIBUTION MAP™ (CAPSTONE WORK)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Brief the activity.
Briefing: each group selects one enterprise Key Result from its Unit 3 Objectives and Key Results that requires contributions from several business functions. It then identifies three or four business functions and completes the six fields for each. Point the groups to the field guidance and to the worked example in part 4.1.

2. Step 1 · Select the enterprise Key Result.
The group’s Objectives and Key Results from Unit 3 are in two drop-down lists on each participant’s page: the Objective first, then its Key Results. For the purposes of the programme, the group selects one enterprise Key Result from its capstone strategy that requires contributions from several business functions.

3. Step 2 · Teach the six fields.
Business Function: The department or function responsible for contributing to the enterprise Key Result.
Required Functional Contribution: The specific result the function must deliver.
People Performance — Required Contribution: The work, results or behaviours expected from individuals and teams.
People Performance — Performance Measure: One or two KPIs, OKRs or observable behavioural measures that demonstrate the required contribution.
Required Organisational Condition: The critical organisational conditions needed to enable performance. Identify the relevant Environment, Systems, Resources or Governance requirements.
Organisational Conditions — Measure or Evidence: A measure or evidence showing whether the required organisational conditions are available and functioning effectively.
Say: "Identify three or four business functions that must contribute to the selected Key Result. For each function, complete the six fields."
The template on each page asks, for each function: What must this function deliver? What must individuals or teams deliver? How will their contribution be measured? What Environment, Systems, Resources or Governance conditions are required? How will the effectiveness or readiness of these conditions be assessed?

4. Read the completion check.
Before proceeding, the group confirms that:
1. Each functional contribution supports the selected enterprise Key Result.
2. People performance expectations are clearly distinguished from organisational enabling conditions.
3. Each contribution has an appropriate measure or evidence of performance.
Output 1: the completed S2R® Contribution Map™.

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants work as a group in Activity 1 of Section 5 of the participant file. This is Capstone work. The group chooses its scribe for this work. The scribe types what the group agrees, and the entries appear on every member’s page.
1. The group chooses an Objective from its Unit 3 OKRs, then one of its Key Results that requires contributions from several business functions, from the two drop-down lists on each page.
2. The group identifies three or four business functions that must contribute to that Key Result.
3. For each function, the group completes the six fields: business function, required functional contribution, people performance required contribution and performance measure, required organisational condition and its measure or evidence.
4. The group reads the completion check, then goes to Activity 2.

slides.title: 5.2 · Activity 2: Apply FACES to your Contribution Map™
slides.notes:
5.2 — ACTIVITY 2: APPLY FACES TO YOUR CONTRIBUTION MAP™ (CAPSTONE WORK)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Brief the activity.
Briefing: each group applies FACES to the contributions it mapped in Activity 1. For each business function it describes one practical management arrangement for each FACES function. Point the groups to the application questions and to the worked example in part 4.2.

The group has established the contributions required to achieve its enterprise Key Result. It now applies FACES to determine how these contributions will be managed. The business functions named in Activity 1 are shown in the FACES template on each participant’s page.

2. Step 3 · Teach the application question for each function.
F · Foster a Results Culture: What routine or leadership practice will reinforce ownership of performance commitments and delivery obstacles? The template asks: How will employees and leaders demonstrate ownership of results?
A · Align Performance: How will the function’s performance expectations and enabling conditions remain connected to the enterprise Key Result? The template asks: How will human contributions and organisational conditions remain aligned with the enterprise Key Result?
C · Create Measurement Transparency: What evidence will make both people performance and organisational constraints visible? The template asks: How will people performance and the effectiveness of the organisational conditions be made visible?
E · Embed Shared Accountability: Who will own performance commitments, enabling conditions and decisions required to address performance gaps? The template asks: Who will be responsible for contributions, enabling conditions and corrective decisions?
S · Support Continuous Development: How will performance findings be used to strengthen employee capability and organisational effectiveness? The template asks: How will performance findings lead to improvements in human capability and organisational conditions?

3. Read the completion check.
Before confirming, the group checks that:
1. All five FACES functions have been addressed for each business function.
2. Your responses describe practical management arrangements.
3. Your FACES application uses the contributions and performance requirements established in Activity 1.
Say: "The S2R® Contribution Map™ establishes the contributions required to achieve an enterprise result. FACES establishes how those contributions will be managed across the organisation. Together, they connect enterprise strategy to functional performance, human contribution, organisational enablement and collective accountability."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants work as a group in Activity 2 of Section 5 of the participant file. This is Capstone work. The group chooses its scribe for this work. The scribe types what the group agrees, and the entries appear on every member’s page.
1. For each business function named in Activity 1, the group describes one practical management arrangement for each of the five FACES functions.
2. The group reads the completion check, then goes to Activity 3.

slides.title: 5.3 · Activity 3: WARD check-up
slides.notes:
5.3 — ACTIVITY 3: WARD · YOUR KEY RESULT’S VITAL CHECK-UP (CAPSTONE WORK)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Open with the check-up.
Say: "Every Key Result your group set in Unit 3 has a baseline, a target and a deadline. Performance management must set out in advance when a Key Result will be checked and which result raises a red flag. Corrective action then starts early, while the gap is still small enough to close. WARD is the vital check-up that sets these points for your Key Result."

2. Teach the four letters.
W · Waypoints: The dates on which the Key Result is checked, and the level it must have reached by each.
A · Alert: How far off a waypoint the result can be before it raises a red flag.
R · Recovery: The corrective action that follows a red flag, for the individuals and for the organisational conditions.
D · Decider: The executive who decides on the recovery and sees it through.

3. Take the worked example through WARD.
Enterprise Key Result from part 4.1: Increase customer enquiries resolved within 48 hours from 65% to 90% by year-end.
W · Waypoints: 72% by the end of March, 80% by the end of June and 85% by the end of September, on the way to 90% at year-end.
A · Alert: More than three percentage points below a waypoint at a monthly review.
R · Recovery · individuals: Team leaders review every open enquiry with its owner each morning, and agents with repeated follow-through gaps are coached.
R · Recovery · organisational conditions: The owner of the condition named in the Contribution Map restores it: IT for system availability, Workforce Planning for staffing coverage, Operations for approval delays.
D · Decider: The Customer Service Executive.
Ask: "At the end of June the result is 74%. What happens on Monday morning, and who decides?"
Guide the groups to see that the waypoint, the alert and the recovery answer the question before the review takes place.

4. Read the completion check.
1. Each waypoint has a date and a level, and the waypoints lead to the target by the deadline.
2. The alert is specific enough that every member reads the same result the same way.
3. The recovery covers the individuals and the organisational conditions named in the Contribution Map.
4. One executive is named as the decider.
Say: "In Unit 8 your group tests its WARD: the alert fires, and you run the recovery."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants work as a group in Activity 3 of Section 5 of the participant file. This is Capstone work. The group chooses its scribe for this work. The scribe types what the group agrees, and the entries appear on every member’s page.
1. The group sets two or three waypoints for its enterprise Key Result: a date and a level for each.
2. The group sets the alert, the recovery for the individuals and for the organisational conditions, and the decider.
3. The group reads the completion check.
4. Each participant reads the record and selects Agree. Print gives a copy.
The agreed record feeds the team’s Capstone Blueprint.

AFTER THE SESSION:
The record reaches you with each participant’s submission, under the heading of Section 5. The agreed record feeds the Unit 6 boxes of the team’s Capstone Blueprint: the Contribution Map in 6A, the FACES application in 6B and the WARD check-up in 6C.

slides.title: Unit Summary · Closing
slides.notes:
UNIT SUMMARY (UNIT 6 SYNTHESIS)

HOW TO TEACH IT:

1. Recap the unit, section by section.
- 1 · Awareness: Performance measurement answers what happened; performance management decides what to do about it. Enterprise performance comes from people performance (results against KPIs and OKRs, and behaviours) and organisational performance (the organisational conditions: environment, systems, resources and governance). The S2R® Contribution Map™ connects an enterprise Key Result to the contribution each function, its people and the organisation must make. FACES names the five functions that manage those contributions across both systems.
- 2 · Intelligence: Performance management is the execution bridge that keeps strategy connected to performance throughout delivery. Four bridges sustain it: Decomposing the Big Picture, Defining the Logic of Success, Calibrating the Rhythm and Structuring the Dialogue. Compliance-driven and commitment-driven architectures shape how accountability works for people and for the organisation when results fall short.
- 3 · Extrapolating: Each executive brings a natural performance focus and a potential blind spot. Unity in Diversity integrates the ten executive performance perspectives into one view of enterprise progress. Three shifts are moving performance management from annual to continuous, from rating-centric to development-centric, and from individual to team performance.
- 4 · Integration: The worked example mapped one enterprise Key Result across Customer Service, IT, Operations and Workforce Planning: each function’s contribution, what its people must deliver and the organisational conditions that enable them, each with a measure or evidence. FACES then showed how those contributions are managed in practice.
- 5 · Application: Each group built an S2R® Contribution Map™ for one of its own enterprise Key Results, applied FACES to manage each function’s contribution and set the WARD check-up for the Key Result. The confirmed record feeds the team’s Capstone Blueprint.

2. Ask the closing question on the slide.
Ask: "Which contribution in your group’s map was hardest to agree, and what does that tell you about the performance management system in your own organisation?" Take an answer from each group.

3. Close the unit.
Say: "A performance management system that only measures has not yet become a management system. The moment measurement becomes the basis for a decision, a conversation, and an accountable intervention — that is the moment execution begins."

4. Say what happens on the portal.
Say: "You now complete the unit on the portal: your four personal reflections and your group’s record in Section 5. When your page is complete, you submit the unit."

ON THE PORTAL, AFTER THE TEACHING:
Participants complete every part of the participant file and submit the unit to the facilitator from the end of Section 5.

AFTER THE SESSION:
Each submission reaches you in the facilitator dashboard. The personal reflections go to each participant’s Learning Portfolio; the group’s confirmed record feeds the team’s Capstone Blueprint.
